title: Chunk, Ship & Measure
objective: After this lesson you will be able to chunk documents with overlap and page metadata, sanity-check retrieval with a TF-IDF cosine baseline, assemble the full five-stage pipeline, and report reject rates and hit-rates honestly.
why: Cleaned text is not yet usable: downstream systems (search, RAG, analytics) consume chunks with provenance, and unmeasured pipelines rot silently. Chunking decides what answers *can* be retrieved; the TF-IDF check proves what *is*; the pipeline report turns a folder of PDFs into a trustworthy dataset with known quality numbers.

blocks.text: A **chunk** is a retrievable unit: bounded size (~200–800 characters for most RAG stacks), **overlap** with neighbors (10–20% so split answers survive), and **metadata** (page_start, page_end, source, section) enabling citations. Never split mid-word; prefer splitting at sentence boundaries when the budget allows; record every boundary decision implicitly via metadata — provenance beats cleverness.

blocks.caption: Budget + sentence-aware cuts + overlap + metadata — the whole chunker

blocks.text: TF-IDF sanity check: retrieval you can reason about

Before embeddings, prove the chunks answer questions with **TF-IDF + cosine similarity**: terms weighted by rarity across chunks, query scored per chunk, top-k returned. It has no synonyms and no semantics — which is exactly why it is the perfect *baseline*: every miss diagnoses cleanly as vocabulary mismatch, boundary split, or missing content (Ch.1 of debugging retrieval). Beat this baseline deliberately or keep it proudly.

blocks.caption: Thirty lines, zero dependencies, fully diagnosable misses

blocks.text: Assemble: the pipeline as a report

The loader runs route → extract → validate → clean → chunk, and its deliverable is numbers: per-stage in/out counts, reject rate with categorized reasons, retrieval hit-rate (gold chunk in top-3) over hand-written questions, and the ugliest artifacts survived. Lead every pipeline conversation with these numbers — '2% rejects (encoding), 8/10 hit-rate' beats any adjective about quality.

blocks.title: Retrieve from chunks
blocks.note: Run it: expect manual#p0 first (refund + policy terms), manual#p2 second (refund only), shipping last at ~0. Then query 'warranty' — zero overlap everywhere — and watch honest zeros: the check reports what the vocabulary supports, nothing more.

items: Chunks: bounded size, 10–20% overlap, page metadata — provenance beats cleverness
TF-IDF + cosine is the diagnosable baseline: misses mean mismatch, boundary, or absence
Pipeline deliverable is numbers: stage counts, reject taxonomy, hit-rate over hand-written questions
Lead with metrics ('2% rejects, 8/10 hits'), never adjectives

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice retrieval and record the full ranking with scores. (b) Add a fourth chunk about 'reimbursement procedures' (no word 'refund') and re-run the 'refund policy' query — record what happens and diagnose it in one sentence. (c) Write the three-line pipeline report for a hypothetical 200-page manual run (invent plausible counts, label them illustrative): stage in/outs, reject taxonomy, hit-rate.
hints: Baseline ranking first: p0 > p2 > p1 with p1 near zero. Scores are cosine similarities, not confidences — read them comparatively.
The reimbursement chunk tests vocabulary mismatch: TF-IDF has no synonyms, so semantically-right-but-lexically-distant chunks score ~0. That sentence is the diagnosis.
Illustrative report shape: '1,840 pages → 1,802 extracted (38 scanned→OCR) → 1,790 validated (12 quarantined: 8 encoding, 4 schema) → 3,412 chunks; hit-rate 8/10; misses: 1 vocabulary, 1 boundary.'
exercise.why: The reimbursement trap teaches TF-IDF's boundary honestly: lexical matching is both the method and the limit. Knowing exactly where the baseline fails is what justifies (or rejects) upgrading to embeddings with cost noted.

options: 0% loses cross-boundary answers; 50% doubles storage for little extra recall — overlap buys boundary survival at bounded linear cost
quiz.explain: Boundary amnesia is the failure (split answers unretrievable); storage is the price. 10–20% is the measured sweet spot — verify per corpus via hit-rate with/without.

quiz.q: TF-IDF check returns zeros for 'warranty' though the manual covers it. Diagnosis?
options: Vocabulary mismatch is one suspect — but first verify the content exists in chunks at all (extraction may have dropped the page); diagnose mismatch vs boundary vs absence in order
quiz.explain: Ordered diagnosis: content present? (extraction), same unit? (boundaries), same words? (vocabulary). Each answer points at a different stage's fix.

options: Source + page span (+ section where available): citations and boundary audits are impossible without provenance
quiz.explain: Retrieval without provenance is trivia: citations need page spans, boundary audits need section info. Metadata is the difference between answers and evidence.

summary: Bound chunks with overlap and metadata, prove retrieval with TF-IDF baselines, diagnose every miss by stage, and ship numbers — stage counts, reject taxonomy, hit-rate. The folder of PDFs is now a dataset with known quality.
